title: What clean code means on a marketing site
excerpt: A maintainable marketing website lets a later editor find the headline, the sections, and the images without a treasure hunt through clever abstractions.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. The editor on the screen is the kind of file a later person has to be able to read.
caption: The page should be findable in the file. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does clean code mean on a marketing site?
faqs.answer: It means a later editor can find the headline, each section, and the images without guessing which file holds them. The page file should read like an outline. Shared sections should be named for their role. Formatting matters less than that map.

faqs.question: Should the homepage live in a CMS or in the repository?
faqs.answer: Put carefully composed pages in the repository when their layout is the design. Put posts, questions, and other repeating text in structured fields when someone who does not open the code will edit them. Both can be clean if there is one list of pages and one list of images.

faqs.question: Does TypeScript make a marketing site easier to keep?
faqs.answer: TypeScript helps when components take named props, because a renamed field fails the build instead of failing in the browser. It does not replace a clear file layout. A well-typed treasure hunt is still a treasure hunt.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A maintainable marketing website is one a later editor can open and change the headline, a section, or an image without a treasure hunt. Clean code, on this kind of site, means the structure of the page is visible in the repository. The words live in an obvious place. The pictures have names a person can recognize.

Hanabi treats clean code as part of the work, next to clarity, a process that can change, speed, and plain communication. On a company site that standard is practical. The next person, who may be the founder six months later, should be able to find the sentence the homepage leads with and replace it before lunch.

## What clean is asking for

A marketing site is a set of pages with a job: explain the offer and give someone a way to respond. The code that serves those pages should read like that description. A route for the homepage. A component for the hero. A component for each repeated section. A single place that holds the image paths.

Clean is a property of that map. When the headline is a string buried inside a styled block three folders down, named after a color, the page is hard to keep. When the headline is a prop called title on a Hero component, the next edit is obvious.

This is a different bar from a library or a backend service. A marketing site does not need a public API with elaborate generics. It needs to stay editable when the offer changes, which it will. The test is a person who was not in the room when the file was written.

## Where the headline, the sections, and the images live

Put the headline in one component, and pass the words in from the page. The page file should read almost like an outline: hero, proof, services, a way to start. Someone skimming the file should be able to point at the line that becomes the first sentence on the screen.

Sections that repeat, such as a row of projects or a list of questions, should be data plus one component. The component knows how to render a row. The data knows what this row says. Changing a sentence means changing the data. Changing the layout of every row means changing the component. Those are different edits, and the files should make the difference obvious.

Images need the same honesty. A file named for the page and the view, stored where that page can find it, beats a hash in a folder called misc. Alt text sits next to the image, because the person who swaps the photo is the person who has to say what is in the frame. On a Hanabi build, marketing image URLs come from one module. Components do not paste bucket domains on their own. When a picture changes, the key changes with it, so a cache cannot keep serving the old bytes under the old name.

Google's guidance on title links is a useful test of the same structure. [Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says each page should have a title element with descriptive text, and one main title that is visually distinct from other headings. The systems that build a title link look at that element, the visible title, and the headings. Three elements fighting to be the title confuse the editor and the search result. One heading, with sections beneath it, is the structure worth keeping.

## What to leave out of the repository

Leave out abstractions that exist for a site you do not have. A generic section renderer that accepts a type string and a bag of unnamed fields feels flexible on day one. Six months later nobody remembers which type draws the quote and which type draws the logos. A named component for each real section makes a longer folder list and a shorter afternoon.

Leave out styles copied from block to block with slightly different spacing. A small set of shared layout components keeps the rhythm. Tailwind fits this when the classes describe the layout on the element you are looking at, and when a pattern is extracted the moment it appears a third time. Pasting a long class string into twelve files is how a simple site becomes a hunt.

Leave out clever loading tricks on a page that is mostly words and pictures. A marketing page can be static. Static means the headline is in the HTML, the sections are in the HTML, and a person reading the response can see the page. Hanabi builds these sites with Next.js and React, and keeps the public pages static where they can be. TypeScript sits on the props so a renamed field fails the build.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) belongs here for a quiet reason. Helpful content is written for people, with a main heading that summarizes the page, produced with care. Code that hides the heading, or generates sections from a pile of unnamed blocks, fights that standard. The person who edits the site is one of the people the structure should serve.

## A path a founder can follow

You do not need to read every component. You need a path.

1. Open the page file for the URL you want to change.
2. Find the section by its name.
3. Edit the words in that section, or the image next to those words.
4. Run the site locally and look at the page at the width you actually use.

If step 2 takes more than a minute, the code is not clean yet, however tidy the formatting is. Formatting is a courtesy. Findability is the requirement.

Name files after the role they play: Hero, ProjectList, IntroCall. Name data after the content: projects, questions, services. Avoid names that describe a moment in the design process. Those names are how a treasure hunt starts.

Comments should be rare. A comment that repeats the component name is noise. A comment that says why a section is static, or why an image is kept out of the CMS, is worth keeping. The why is the part the next person cannot see from the markup.

Keep a short note at the top of the page file if the outline is not obvious from the component names alone. Two lines are enough: what this URL is for, and which component holds the first sentence. That note is for the editor, not for the visitor.

## What you should be able to change without a call

Some changes belong in code, and some belong in a CMS. The split should be deliberate. The headline, the section order, and the images on a carefully composed homepage often belong in code, because their layout is the design. A blog post, a question, or a project blurb that will be edited by someone who does not open the repository belongs in a structured field.

Either way, the map is the same. There is a list of pages, a list of sections, and a list of images. A content model that mirrors that list is clean. A content model that exposes every margin as a field is a page builder wearing a different name. Editors need the things that change. They need the headline, the proof, and the picture. They do not need a control for every pixel.

When the engagement ends, this map is part of what you should own. The repository should build on a machine that is yours, with a readme that names the command to run the site and the command to build it. Secrets stay in an environment file that is not committed. The next person should not have to ask which folder is the real homepage.

The next piece is about that ownership: [what you should own after a studio build](/blog/what-you-own-after-a-studio-build). It covers the repository, the domain, and the logins that make the clean structure actually yours.

If you want the site built so the next edit is obvious, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio designs and builds the page, and leaves the code in a shape a later editor can follow.
